title: Quantifying Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation in the Presence of Domain Shift
claim: Excess risk varies non-monotonically with a control parameter, and there is a regime where the transferred model beats the baseline despite domain shift.
layout: 2 stacked panels, top-to-bottom, shared x-axis, theory curves with simulation markers
description: Two vertically stacked line plots share the x-axis ξ, which runs from about -0.1 to 1.1. The y-axis is Excess Risk. Panel (a), captioned 'Model shift', compares two ‖γ‖ values, 0.63 in navy and 0.89 in orange. Panel (b), captioned 'Covariate shift', compares covariance Σ1 in navy and a tilde-Σ1 variant in orange. In both panels, solid theory curves are overlaid with blue circle and red square simulation markers that sit close to them. Each curve is U-shaped, with a minimum near ξ≈0.4–0.5. A green dashed horizontal line marks the ridge (student-only) baseline at about 0.9. The curves fall below the baseline for intermediate ξ and rise above it at large ξ. The eye goes first to the U-shaped curves crossing the green line. A legend sits in the top-left corner of each panel.
caption: Excess risk in the presence of domain shift. Solid lines
abstract: This paper presents a theoretical investigation into the generalization capabilities of cross-domain knowledge distillation. Utilizing a high-dimensional asymptotic analysis of a linear teacher–student model, we characterize the excess risk while accounting for both model and covariate shifts. Our results provide a formal guarantee for the efficacy of distillation: even when the source and target domains differ substantially, there still may exist a regime where the student model achieves superior generalization ability over the student-only baseline. Moreover, we identify a \textit{crossed double descent} phenomenon: the excess risk can vary non-monotonically with the teacher’s and student’s dimension-to-sample-size ratios. These results provide rigorous insight into when and why distillation helps across domains.
